analysis.one_liner: Charges a rising fee on carbon pollution and returns most of the money to workers, seniors, and low-income households.
analysis.headline: The carbon fee bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 2018 and never advanced further before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a per-ton fee on coal, oil, and natural gas based on the carbon dioxide they produce when burned, starting at $50 per ton in 2019 and rising each year. It would also charge fees on other greenhouse gases and on methane leaked or vented in fuel production. The money would be returned largely to the public: up to $800 per worker through a refundable tax credit, payments to Social Security and veterans' beneficiaries, and grants to states to help low-income and rural households with energy costs and to retrain fossil fuel workers. It also includes border adjustments so imported goods pay a comparable fee and exporters get refunds, and it would reduce the corporate income tax rate. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Working taxpayers would receive a refundable credit of up to $800 per year ($1,600 for couples). Social Security beneficiaries, eligible veterans, and disabled individuals would receive a matching annual payment. Low-income households would get monthly rebates through state programs, and states would receive $10 billion per year to help low-income and rural households with energy costs and to retrain fossil fuel workers. Everyone would benefit from reduced carbon emissions, since the fee is designed to keep rising until national emissions fall to 20 percent of their 2005 level.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, seniors, low-income and rural households

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a fee per ton of carbon dioxide emitted by coal, petroleum products, and natural gas, starting at $50 in 2019 and rising annually, plus fees on fluorinated greenhouse gases, methane and leakage across fuel supply chains, and a methane-specific surcharge after 2021.
Creates a refundable carbon fee offset credit of up to $800 per worker ($1,600 for joint filers), which the bill exempts from counting as income for federal benefit eligibility.

Sends equal payments to Social Security beneficiaries, eligible veterans, and disabled individuals who cannot claim the worker credit, and gives states $10 billion a year in grants for low-income household energy rebates, rural assistance, and job training prioritized for fossil-fuel workers.
Provides refunds for captured and stored carbon dioxide and requires Treasury to publicly disclose revenues and benefits through a dedicated website.

analysis.who_pays: Producers and importers of coal, oil, natural gas, and fluorinated gases would pay the fees, but they would pass much of that cost to consumers through higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. Corporate taxpayers would benefit from the corporate rate cut the bill's title calls for. Households that use large amounts of energy but receive no credit or rebate — roughly middle- and upper-income non-filers and businesses — would bear the fee's cost directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy consumers and fossil fuel producers

drawbacks.text: Fossil fuel fees are levied at the point of production or import, so companies can pass them to consumers in the form of higher gasoline, heating, and electricity prices before any rebate arrives.

The bill's stated purposes include reducing the corporate income tax rate, meaning a portion of the carbon fee revenue would be directed toward cutting corporate taxes rather than solely returning money to households.
The fee applies to natural gas and covers venting, flaring, and leakage across fuel supply chains, which raises costs for home heating in regions dependent on gas even after the fixed $800 credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy design is defensible: a rising carbon price with refunds to workers, seniors, and low-income households offsets most of the regressive cost, border adjustments protect domestic manufacturers, and public revenue disclosure adds transparency. The main drawbacks are honest ones — energy costs rise before rebates arrive, natural gas is a large emissions source that fees push consumers away from, and the bill's stated purpose of cutting the corporate income tax rate would route some revenue toward corporations. But the bill never advanced beyond a Senate referral, so none of these tradeoffs was ever tested on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a markup, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on February 5, 2018.
On the same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and other carbon-intensive industries are better off because the carbon fee never became law; no industry had to pay the emissions fees. Households and future beneficiaries of cleaner air and climate stability are worse off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers; no carbon fees were ever paid

against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 5, 2018 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Fossil fuel and allied industry groups
against.what_they_did: Fossil fuel interests have consistently opposed carbon pricing legislation in Congress, though no specific lobbying on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Democratic sponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and with a Senate controlled by Republicans and a Finance Committee chaired by a Republican, it never moved.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: The bill charges these industries per ton of carbon dioxide their products emit, plus a surcharge for methane and leaks in their supply chains, and forces public reporting of those emissions. This directly threatens the revenue of fossil fuel producers, which is the point of the policy.
They pay more for fossil fuel inputs but receive refunds on exports and equivalency fees on competing imports, largely insulating them from foreign competition under the carbon price.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and clean energy industries
industries.note: Refunds for captured carbon dioxide and rising fossil fuel costs create new demand for capture technology, renewables, and low-carbon goods.
